# **Temporal Graph Networks: Exhaustive Architectural Analysis and Pathways to State-Space Hypergraphs for Provenance Data**

## **Introduction to Continuous-Time Dynamic Graph Representation**

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have fundamentally redefined the boundaries of representation learning, enabling the robust modeling of complex relational structures across domains as diverse as biological interactomes, financial transaction networks, and natural language processing.1 However, the foundational architectures of traditional GNNs—such as Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and standard Graph Attention Networks (GATs)—operate under the restrictive assumption that the underlying graph topology and the associated node features are static.2 In reality, the most critical data structures in computer science and network theory are inherently dynamic. Real-world systems, particularly digital infrastructure, operating system provenance logs, and cyber-security threat vectors, evolve continuously through high-velocity streams of timestamped events.  
To address the limitations of static graph modeling, the paradigm of dynamic graph representation learning emerged. This domain is broadly bifurcated into two distinct methodological approaches: Discrete-Time Dynamic Graphs (DTDGs) and Continuous-Time Dynamic Graphs (CTDGs).4 Early models relied heavily on the DTDG approach, which conceptualizes the temporal evolution of a graph as a sequence of discrete, static snapshots taken at regular, predefined intervals.4 While computationally straightforward and compatible with existing static GNN architectures, the snapshot-based approach suffers from a catastrophic flaw: it inevitably destroys fine-grained temporal ordering within the snapshot windows.7 If multiple events occur within the same discrete window, their chronological sequence is flattened, erasing the precise causality of the interactions. Furthermore, determining the optimal snapshot interval requires significant domain-specific heuristics, creating an inescapable trade-off between temporal resolution and computational overhead.  
In stark contrast, CTDGs represent networks as an asynchronous stream of timestamped events, preserving the exact temporal resolution of every interaction without introducing artificial discretization artifacts.2 The Temporal Graph Network (TGN) framework, introduced by Rossi et al. (2020), represents a seminal advancement in CTDG modeling. By elegantly combining persistent memory modules with graph-based temporal attention operators, TGN established a generic, highly efficient framework for deep learning on dynamic graphs.1 It introduced the concept of continuously updating node representations by maintaining an internal state (memory) for every node, modified asynchronously whenever an event occurs.2  
This report delivers an exhaustive architectural analysis of the TGN framework. It deconstructs the precise mechanics of its memory update protocols, message computation and aggregation strategies, continuous-time encoding formulations, and its strict chronological training procedures. Furthermore, this report critically evaluates the fundamental limitations of the TGN framework. These limitations—most notably its rigid restriction to pairwise interactions, its reliance on computationally bottlenecked recurrent memory updaters, and its vulnerability to catastrophic precision loss when processing data at nanosecond granularities—serve as the analytical foundation for proposing an advanced, next-generation architecture. This proposed architectural paradigm leverages State-Space Models (specifically the Mamba architecture) and hypergraph topology to effectively model system provenance data, moving decisively beyond the theoretical constraints of standard Temporal Graph Networks.

## **The TGN Architecture: An Exhaustive Breakdown**

The TGN operates as a sophisticated encoder-decoder framework engineered explicitly for continuous-time event streams.2 The fundamental input to this architecture is a monotonically increasing sequence of timestamped events. These events can manifest either as node-wise feature updates (e.g., a node altering its attributes at a specific time) or as pairwise interaction events (e.g., a directed edge forming between a source node and a destination node).2  
The primary objective of the TGN encoder is to produce a temporally aware, context-rich node embedding, denoted as ![][image1], for any given node ![][image2] at any specified continuous timestamp ![][image3].2 This embedding must encapsulate both the structural topology of the node's neighborhood and the precise temporal history of its past interactions. To achieve this synthesis of structure and time, TGN relies on a highly orchestrated sequence of differentiable operations that update a node's historical context immediately before predicting its future state.

### **State Persistence: The Memory Module and Update Mechanism**

The defining characteristic and primary innovation of the TGN architecture is its maintenance of a persistent, per-node memory state, formally denoted as ![][image4]. This memory vector serves as a compressed, latent representation of the node's entire historical interaction trajectory up to time ![][image3].2 It is critical to distinguish this memory state from traditional node embeddings. While static node embeddings are generally learned parameters optimized across the entire dataset, the memory ![][image4] in TGN is an explicit, continuously evolving state vector that is dynamically updated during both the forward pass of the training phase and during live inference.2  
When a node ![][image2] is involved in an event at time ![][image3], its memory must be updated to integrate this novel information. This state transition is governed by a learnable memory update function, which fuses the new event data—structured as an aggregated message, ![][image5]—with the node's prior memory state ![][image6].11 The notation ![][image7] is utilized to denote the memory state of the node immediately prior to the current event, ensuring strict temporal causality.  
The fundamental memory update equation is mathematically formulated as:  
![][image8]  
In the canonical implementations of TGN, the ![][image9] function is realized using a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) cell, specifically defaulting to a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) or, alternatively, a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network.2 The GRU is generally prioritized in empirical deployments due to its streamlined gating mechanism, which provides comparable representational capacity to the LSTM but with significantly reduced computational overhead and parameter counts.2  
The operational mechanics of the GRU-based memory update follow a highly structured gating sequence. First, an update gate is computed to determine the precise extent to which the previous memory state ![][image6] should be retained versus overwritten by the incoming aggregated message ![][image5]. Simultaneously, a reset gate determines how much of the historical memory ought to be forgotten or suppressed before computing the new potential state. Using the output of the reset gate and the incoming message, a candidate memory state is generated. Finally, the ultimate memory state ![][image4] is calculated as a linear interpolation between the previous memory state and the candidate state, strictly dictated by the coefficients of the update gate.  
This recurrent formulation guarantees that the memory state maintains a persistent, albeit decaying, record of all prior interactions. It grants the TGN the theoretical capability to memorize long-term dependencies for every single node in the network.2 At initialization (time ![][image10]), the memory for all nodes is instantiated as a zero vector. As events stream through the network, these vectors diverge and evolve, capturing the unique behavioral footprint of each entity.

### **Message Computation and Intra-Batch Aggregation**

Before the GRU memory update function can process new interaction data, the raw event parameters must be translated into a standardized, mathematically rigorous message format. This translation is executed by two distinct but complementary modules: the message function and the message aggregator.

#### **Pairwise Message Computation**

In the standard TGN paradigm, interactions are strictly conceptualized as pairwise topological events occurring between a source node ![][image2] and a destination node ![][image11] at a specific continuous time ![][image3], frequently accompanied by an arbitrary vector of edge features ![][image12].2 When such an interaction transpires, the architecture dictates that a message must be computed for both nodes involved, as the state of both entities is fundamentally altered by the interaction.  
A critical design choice in the TGN framework is the formulation of these messages. The message is not merely a transformation of the raw interaction features. Instead, the computation explicitly mandates the inclusion of the *current memory states of both the source and the destination nodes*.11

In these equations, ![][image15] represents the exact temporal duration elapsed since the respective node's last recorded interaction. The functions ![][image16] and ![][image17] are learnable neural transformations, typically instantiated as Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs). The theoretical brilliance of this formulation lies in the cross-pollination of states. By explicitly incorporating the destination node's previous memory ![][image18] into the message generated for the source node ![][image2], the architecture allows node ![][image2] to absorb the historical context of the entity it is interacting with. This mechanism is the primary vehicle for structural information to propagate through the network over continuous time.  
However, in many practical and computationally optimized implementations of TGN (including several benchmarked in the original paper), the message function is simplified to a non-learnable identity function.11 The identity function simply concatenates the input vectors: $$. This concatenation preserves all raw informational entropy without introducing additional parameters, allowing downstream modules to determine the relative importance of the historical states versus the edge features.

#### **Temporal Message Aggregation**

A fundamental engineering reality of training deep learning models on continuous-time graphs is the absolute necessity of batch processing.12 Processing events strictly sequentially, one by one, is computationally prohibitive and entirely fails to leverage the highly parallelized architecture of modern GPUs.12  
However, temporal batching introduces a structural complication. Within a single temporal batch window, a highly active node ![][image2] might be involved in multiple distinct, chronologically ordered events at timestamps ![][image19] (where all timestamps are ![][image20]). Because each of these events generates an individual message, and because the subsequent memory update function (the GRU) is designed to operate on single sequential state transitions, feeding multiple concurrent messages for the same node into the memory updater simultaneously is mathematically impossible.  
To resolve this bottleneck, an intermediate mechanism is required to aggregate all messages directed at a specific node within the current batch into a single, unified tensor. The message aggregator combines all messages for node ![][image2] into an aggregated message ![][image5] 11:  
![][image21]  
While the ![][image22] function could theoretically be implemented as a complex learnable module—such as an intra-batch attention mechanism or an internal RNN—the canonical TGN framework opts for simplistic, non-learnable aggregators to maximize computational throughput and prevent severe latency during the forward pass.11  
The structural characteristics of the two primary message aggregators utilized in TGN are detailed below:

| Aggregation Strategy | Mathematical Formulation | Operational Characteristic | Theoretical Limitation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Mean Message** | **![][image23]** | Averages all message vectors for node ![][image2] in the batch. | Destroys the temporal ordering and relative causality of rapid, sequential interactions within the batch. |
| **Most Recent Message** | **![][image24]** (where ![][image25] is the latest time) | Discards all earlier messages and retains only the chronologically latest message. | Discards potentially critical topological information from earlier interactions within the batch window. |

This required aggregation step represents a profound theoretical bottleneck in continuous-time modeling. While strictly necessary for parallel processing, both the mean and most-recent aggregators result in a fundamental loss of high-resolution sequential information within the batch window, smoothing over the exact micro-dynamics of high-frequency node interactions.

### **The Mathematics of Continuous Time Encoding**

Operating on a continuous-time dynamic graph relies entirely on the precise and mathematically sound encoding of timestamps. Standard self-attention mechanisms, MLPs, and graph convolutions are inherently permutation-invariant; they possess no innate understanding of time, duration, or sequential ordering.14 To contextualize node interactions properly, the TGN framework integrates sophisticated temporal encoding mechanisms that map scalar time values (specifically, the time interval ![][image15]) into high-dimensional vector spaces.3  
The primary theoretical challenge necessitating temporal encoding is the phenomenon of **memory staleness**.11 Consider a scenario where a node undergoes a flurry of interactions and then remains inactive for an extended period. During this latency, the node's memory state ![][image6] becomes frozen and increasingly disconnected from the current, evolved context of the broader network.11 When predicting a new interaction for this long-inactive node, the model cannot simply rely on the stale memory; it must mathematically adjust the representation to reflect the profound passage of time.

#### **Harmonic Time Encoding via Bochner's Theorem**

To rigorously address time embedding, TGN predominantly utilizes a generic, continuous time encoding function, denoted as ![][image26]. This formulation was originally conceptualized in the Temporal Graph Attention (TGAT) architecture by Xu et al. (2020) and serves as the temporal backbone for the attention-based variants of TGN.11  
This encoding mechanism leverages Bochner's theorem from harmonic analysis. Bochner's theorem establishes that any positive-definite, continuous, translation-invariant kernel can be uniquely represented as the Fourier transform of a positive finite Borel measure.14 In the context of continuous-time representation learning, this theorem provides a rigorous theoretical foundation for mapping a scalar time interval ![][image15] into a functional, continuous feature space that preserves relative temporal distances.  
The resulting time encoding takes the form of a vector composed of learnable trigonometric functions:  
![][image27]  
where ![][image28] represents the fixed dimensionality of the time encoding vector, and ![][image29] are learnable frequency parameters optimized via backpropagation.10  
This harmonic vector is inextricably integrated into the computation of the Temporal Graph Attention (attn) module within the TGN embedding generation phase.11 When computing the attention weights between a target query node ![][image2] and its temporal neighborhood ![][image30], the attention mechanism evaluates both the structural node features and the harmonic encoding of the elapsed time since their specific interaction, ![][image31].11  
By projecting time into this trigonometric space, the multi-head attention mechanism can dynamically assign differential importance to neighbors based on temporal proximity. It allows the model to learn complex, non-monotonic periodicities—recognizing, for instance, that interactions occurring exactly 24 hours ago might be more relevant than interactions occurring 12 hours ago, depending on the optimized frequencies ![][image32]. This capability effectively circumvents the memory staleness problem by forcing the attention module to re-evaluate the relevance of a node's historical state relative to the current continuous timestamp.11

#### **Linear Time Projection (The JODIE Mechanism)**

As a computationally streamlined alternative to harmonic temporal attention, the TGN framework also supports a direct Time Projection mechanism, an approach originally pioneered in the JODIE framework (Kumar et al., 2019).5  
Instead of feeding elapsed time encodings into a computationally expensive multi-head attention layer, this method applies a direct, parameterized mathematical transformation to the node's stale memory vector, mathematically projecting it forward in time to the current timestamp ![][image3] 11:  
![][image33]  
In this formulation, ![][image15] is the elapsed time since the node's last recorded interaction, ![][image34] represents a learned weight vector of the same dimensionality as the memory state, and the operator ![][image35] denotes the Hadamard (element-wise) product.11 While this linear projection is exceptionally efficient and minimizes computational latency, it is structurally less expressive than harmonic attention. It forces a strictly linear, monotonic evolution of the memory state, making it fundamentally incapable of modeling complex periodic temporal patterns or cyclical behaviors inherent in many dynamic systems.20

### **Chronological Optimization and the Information Leakage Paradox**

Training a highly parameterized dynamic graph neural network on a continuous stream of events introduces unique architectural and algorithmic challenges that are entirely absent in the training of static GNNs. Chief among these is the strict requirement for temporal causality and the prevention of catastrophic information leakage.11

#### **The Absolute Necessity of Chronological Batching**

In standard, static graph learning environments, nodes or subgraphs can be batched randomly. This random shuffling ensures that optimization steps are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), which stabilizes gradient descent and accelerates convergence. In continuous-time TGNs, this practice is mathematically invalid and fundamentally destructive.  
The data in a CTDG contains strict, unyielding sequential dependencies. The state of node ![][image36] at time ![][image37] is a direct, cumulative result of its interactions at times ![][image38] through ![][image39]. Processing these interactions in randomly sampled batches would irreparably fracture the temporal flow, causing the recurrent memory states to become temporally incoherent and effectively meaningless.11 Consequently, TGN enforces a strict protocol of chronological batching. The training algorithm sweeps through the temporal timeline, slicing the dataset and processing batches of events strictly in the exact order they occurred.11  
Empirical studies by the TGN authors indicate that a batch size of approximately 200 interactions provides the optimal theoretical balance.11 If batches are excessively large, the intra-batch message aggregation phase becomes overly aggressive (collapsing hundreds of sequential messages for a single node into one mean vector, destroying sequential nuance), and predictions at the tail end of the batch are computed using memory states that have not been updated since the batch commenced.11 Conversely, extremely small batches cripple GPU utilization, stalling parallel processing capabilities and leading to intractable training times.11

#### **The Information Leakage Paradox**

The most intricate engineering challenge within TGN's training procedure involves ensuring that the memory-related modules (the message function, the aggregator, and the GRU updater) receive gradients without causing temporal data leakage.11  
Consider the naive approach: an interaction ![][image12] occurs in the training set. One might intuitively update the memories of node ![][image2] and node ![][image11] with the features of this interaction, and *then* use these updated memories to compute the probability of the edge existing in order to calculate the Binary Cross-Entropy loss.  
However, doing so means the decoder is attempting to predict an event using memory states that have *already been updated with the very event it is trying to predict*.11 This constitutes textbook information leakage. The model effectively looks into the future, resulting in an artificially near-zero training loss and catastrophic generalization failure during inductive inference on unseen data.  
To solve this paradox, the memory-related modules must be updated using past events, but these modules must remain attached to the PyTorch computational graph so that when the loss is calculated on *current* events, the gradients flow backward through the memory modules.11

#### **The Raw Message Store Mechanism**

To achieve this delicate balance, TGN introduces the **Raw Message Store**.11 This module serves as a staging area to artificially delay memory updates to subsequent batches, ensuring temporal causality while preserving gradient flow.  
The chronological training loop for a given batch operates through the following strictly ordered protocol 11:

1. **Memory Update via Delayed Messages:** At the very beginning of the batch computation, before any predictions are made, the model retrieves raw messages from the Raw Message Store. Crucially, these messages were generated by interactions that occurred in *previous* batches.11 The memory updater (GRU) processes these delayed messages to bring the memory states ![][image40] and ![][image41] up to the chronological boundary of the current batch.  
2. **Embedding Generation and Target Prediction:** Using these newly updated (but strictly pre-current-batch) memory states, the embedding module computes the continuous-time node representations.11 Negative sampling is performed to generate false edges. The decoder then predicts the probabilities of both the true positive interactions occurring in the *current* batch, alongside the negative samples.11 At this exact moment, the model has absolutely no knowledge of the current batch's topological features.  
3. **Loss Calculation and Backpropagation:** The Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) loss is computed based on the decoder's predictions.11 Because the memory update step (Step 1\) occurred within the same automatic differentiation computational graph prior to the loss calculation, Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) executes successfully. The gradient flows backward from the loss, through the predicted embeddings, and directly into the memory updater, the message aggregator, and the message functions.11  
4. **State Detachment and Populating the Store:** Once gradients are calculated, the memory states must be detached from the computational graph to prevent the graph from growing infinitely over the sequence of batches (which would cause Out-Of-Memory errors).22 Finally, the interactions from the *current* batch are converted into raw messages and written into the Raw Message Store.11 They will remain dormant in this queue until they are retrieved to update the memory at the beginning of the *next* chronological batch.

This elegantly engineered delay mechanism ensures that the temporal causality of the continuous-time graph is preserved, actively preventing the decoder from accessing future topological data while seamlessly allowing the state-tracking modules to be trained end-to-end.11

## **Structural and Theoretical Limitations of TGN**

Despite definitively establishing the benchmark for continuous-time dynamic graph learning and proving the viability of explicit state tracking, the TGN framework exhibits several structural, computational, and theoretical limitations. A rigorous understanding of these weaknesses is paramount when designing advanced architectures for complex, high-velocity datasets, particularly in domains requiring absolute precision like cybersecurity and system provenance tracking.

### **1\. Memory Scalability and State Explosion**

The TGN framework mandates the initialization and continuous maintenance of a persistent, high-dimensional, GPU-resident memory vector for every single node in the graph.12 In enterprise applications involving massive graphs with tens of millions of nodes (such as global transaction networks or data center provenance logs), this ![][image42] memory footprint causes severe bottlenecking and rapid memory explosion.12  
Furthermore, during the inference phase, the arrival of a single new edge triggers an extensive cascade of embedding updates. The memory state must be read from the GPU, updated via the GRU utilizing the message aggregator, and subsequently rewritten. This creates intense I/O pressure, leading to prohibitive latency issues in real-time streaming environments.12 While auxiliary optimization systems like StreamTGN have attempted to mitigate this through the use of dirty-flag propagation (updating only the affected local neighborhood), the fundamental architectural requirement of a monolithic, per-node state matrix remains a structural hindrance to hyperscale deployment.12

### **2\. Vulnerability to Long-Term Dependency Degradation**

TGN relies almost exclusively on recurrent neural network architectures (specifically GRUs or LSTMs) to power its memory updates.2 It is extensively documented in deep sequence modeling literature that RNNs fundamentally suffer from the vanishing and exploding gradient problem when tasked with processing extremely long sequences.20  
In highly active dynamic graphs, a single node (such as a core operating system process or a heavily trafficked web server) may participate in tens or hundreds of thousands of interactions over its lifecycle. The standard GRU mechanism intrinsically struggles to maintain highly specific historical context over these protracted temporal horizons. As new events continuously trigger the update gate, older, potentially critical information is gradually compressed, diluted, and ultimately overridden by high-frequency noise.23 While the attention-based modules utilized in TGAT attempt to mitigate this by allowing the model to look back at past neighbors, the underlying central memory state itself still decays, severely limiting the model's ability to recognize long-term periodic anomalies or multi-stage systemic patterns.20

### **3\. The Constraint of Pairwise Interactions**

A profound theoretical limitation of the canonical TGN architecture is its rigid, mathematical adherence to pairwise interactions.2 The message function, defined as ![][image43], strictly operates on an edge connecting exactly two nodes.  
However, many real-world complex systems cannot be accurately or comprehensively modeled as simple bipartite or homogeneous pairwise graphs. This is acutely true in operating system provenance tracking. In provenance data, a system event often encompasses multiple interacting entities simultaneously. For instance, a single system call might involve a specific User executing a Process that simultaneously modifies a shared Network Socket and appends data to a local File.  
Forcing these intrinsically multi-entity relationships into independent, disjointed pairwise edges (e.g., creating separate edges for Process-Socket and Process-File) destroys the atomic context of the event. It severs the unified flow of state propagation. TGN cannot natively comprehend that the state of the File and the state of the Socket were altered by the exact same atomic operation, isolating their memory updates and blinding the model to complex, coordinated topological structures.

### **4\. Granularity Limits of Harmonic Time Encoding**

The Bochner's theorem-based temporal encoding, utilizing sinusoidal functions ![][image44], excels at general temporal scaling but falters dramatically at extreme granularities.20  
When analyzing ultra-fast data streams with nanosecond precision (such as kernel-level system logs), the input time interval ![][image15] can vary by extreme orders of magnitude—ranging from ![][image45] seconds (consecutive CPU instructions) to hundreds of thousands of seconds (days between user logins).26 Passing raw, unscaled, or vastly varying nanosecond floating-point values into fixed harmonic frequencies ![][image32] leads to numerical instability. It induces catastrophic cancellation, floating-point overflow, and aliasing issues, resulting in a complete failure to disentangle highly localized temporal signals.24  
While learnable generalized time encodings (LeTE) utilizing Fourier series or B-splines offer slightly more functional flexibility, the fundamental mathematical rigidity of projecting precise, sub-microsecond intervals through cyclic trigonometric boundaries remains a severe bottleneck for extremely fine-grained anomaly detection.29

## **Architectural Evolution: Pathways to Continuous State-Space Hypergraphs**

The detailed mechanics, coupled with the identified theoretical and practical limitations of the TGN framework, directly inform the stringent design requirements for novel, highly specialized dynamic graph architectures. Specifically, when the objective is to model system provenance data—which is characterized by dense hyper-connectivity, continuous state propagation across shared objects, extremely long chronological sequences, and exact nanosecond timestamp precision—the canonical TGN must be heavily adapted, dismantled, and evolved.  
By deconstructing the specific mechanisms TGN utilizes to accomplish state tracking (per-node GRU memory) and interaction routing (pairwise message passing), we can articulate a fundamentally more expressive framework. This proposed evolution abandons standard graphs and RNNs, instead utilizing continuous State-Space Models (SSMs) mapped over dynamic hypergraph topologies.

### **From Pairwise Edges to Stateful Hyperedges**

The success of TGN demonstrates unequivocally that maintaining an explicit, per-node memory state is a highly powerful mechanism for compressing historical trajectories in continuous time.2 However, as established, TGN restricts this state exchange strictly to the source and destination nodes of a standard, binary edge.11  
In the context of provenance data, system operations are rarely purely pairwise. A system call is an event that binds an executing Process, an authorizing User, a target File, and a Network Socket into a single, indivisible atomic action.27 To model this relational complexity accurately, the architecture must abandon standard graph topology in favor of **hypergraphs**, where a single hyperedge can connect an arbitrary number of nodes (![][image46]) simultaneously.  
To facilitate this, the message generation framework must be radically redesigned. Instead of TGN's binary pairwise message generation:  
![][image47]  
The proposed hyperedge architecture requires a message function that pools, aligns, and computes the interactive state of *all* entities participating in the atomic event concurrently:  
![][image48]  
Crucially, this structural expansion allows internal state to propagate continuously across entities through shared objects. In a standard TGN, if Process A modifies File X at ![][image38], and later Process B reads File X at ![][image49], the sequential dependency provided to Process B relies entirely and exclusively on the isolated memory state of File X.11  
By extending the architecture to utilize hyperedges and holistic event-message pooling, the system can dynamically route the complex, multi-dimensional memory state of Process A *through* the shared object (File X) and directly into the memory update formulation of Process B during subsequent hyper-interactions. This creates a highly responsive, deeply cross-pollinated state representation that captures systemic contagion and causality in a way that TGN's isolated, pairwise updates fundamentally cannot achieve.

### **Resolving Memory Degradation with Continuous State-Space Models (SSMs)**

As analyzed previously, TGN’s utilization of GRUs subjects it to the vanishing gradient problem, crippling its ability to track long-term dependencies over extended sequences of high-frequency provenance logs.20 Furthermore, the inherently sequential nature of RNNs prevents the parallelization of the memory update across the time dimension, slowing training significantly.8  
Replacing the GRU with a continuous-time State Space Model (SSM), explicitly leveraging the Mamba architecture, directly and mathematically resolves these limitations.23 Mamba translates the dynamic graph modeling paradigm into a structured, long-term sequence modeling problem, providing both linear time complexity and infinite sequence context.23  
A core theoretical advantage of the SSM framework over the GRU in TGN is its mathematical foundation in continuous differential systems. An SSM inherently maps a one-dimensional input sequence ![][image50] to an output ![][image51] through a continuous hidden state ![][image52]:  
![][image53]  
![][image54]  
To operate on discrete, digital graph events, these continuous parameters (![][image36] and ![][image55]) must be mathematically discretized using a specifically calculated step size, denoted as ![][image56], yielding discrete matrices ![][image57] and ![][image58].8  
In novel architectures like DyG-Mamba (Dynamic Graph Mamba), the timespan between graph events (![][image15]) is not merely fed as a raw numerical feature into a neural network (as is done in TGN). Instead, the exact timespan is fundamentally utilized as the control signal for the mathematical discretization step ![][image56].23  
This continuous differential formulation allows the Mamba-based memory updater to dynamically adjust the retention, integration, or forgetting of historical information based on the exact temporal gap, mimicking the theoretical Ebbinghaus forgetting curve natively within the matrix algebra.23 Because the Mamba architecture utilizes a hardware-aware selective scan mechanism, it can process these dynamic memory updates with strict ![][image59] linear time complexity while maintaining full parallelization across the sequence.8 This enables the hypergraph architecture to process vastly longer sequences of provenance logs without the gradual memory decay and computational lag inherent in TGN's GRU.

### **Mastering Nanosecond Precision via SSM Discretization**

The temporal encoding utilized within TGN relies entirely on mapping the scalar value ![][image15] into a high-dimensional space via trigonometric functions derived from Bochner’s theorem.14 In the specific context of analyzing nanosecond provenance timestamps, raw ![][image15] inputs can be infinitesimally small (e.g., ![][image45] seconds between subsequent hardware interrupts).26  
Utilizing these extreme values in a standard TGN harmonic encoder requires aggressive normalization, logarithmic scaling, and clipping; otherwise, the cosine and sine mappings fail to differentiate between rapidly occurring micro-events due to float64 precision limits in the embedding space.24 If the difference between ![][image38] and ![][image49] is 5 nanoseconds, a trigonometric projection may map both to an identical vector representation, completely destroying the temporal causality required to detect ultra-fast race conditions or multi-stage malware execution.  
By integrating the Mamba SSM formulation, the architecture bypasses the reliance on, and the pitfalls of, harmonic encoding entirely. Instead of mapping ![][image15] into a static spatial vector to be concatenated with node features, the timespan ![][image15] directly and dynamically informs the parameterization of the state transition matrix ![][image57].8  
The timespan function controlling ![][image56] can be made explicitly learnable and monotonically increasing. For example, the transformation can be parameterized as:  
![][image60]  
This formulation allows the dynamic system to automatically learn how to compress or expand historical information across vastly different time scales natively within the state update, without requiring spatial embedding.34  
This continuous differential approach is theoretically superior for nanosecond data. It does not force the concept of "time elapsed" into a rigid, lossy spatial representation. Rather, it allows the passage of time to act as a continuous decay and integration operator over the hidden state ![][image52], maintaining absolute numerical stability and high-resolution differentiation even at the nanosecond scale.

### **Comparative Architectural Synthesis**

To summarize the strategic pivot from the standard Temporal Graph Network to the proposed continuous State-Space Hypergraph, the core architectural distinctions and theoretical upgrades can be structured as follows:

| Architectural Component | Canonical TGN Architecture | Proposed State-Space Hypergraph | Theoretical Advantage for Provenance |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Network Topology** | Strict Pairwise graphs (binary edges between source and destination). | Hypergraphs (N-ary entity relationships encompassing multiple nodes). | Accurately models atomic system calls involving users, processes, files, and sockets simultaneously. |
| **State Propagation** | Exchanged strictly between interacting node ![][image2] and node ![][image11]. | Propagated fluidly across all involved entities via shared structural objects. | Captures deep, multi-hop systemic contagion and causality sequences. |
| **Memory Updater** | GRU / LSTM (Recurrent Neural Networks). | Mamba (Selective State Space Model based on continuous differential equations). | Eliminates vanishing gradients; allows for theoretically infinite chronological sequence tracking. |
| **Time Complexity** | **![][image59]** sequential (bottlenecked by unrollable GRU recurrence). | ![][image59] parallelized (utilizing hardware-aware Selective Scan algorithms). | Unlocks hyperscale processing capabilities for massive data center logs. |
| **Temporal Encoding** | Harmonic/Bochner trigonometric vectors mapped to spatial dimensions. | Continuous ![][image15] utilized directly as the state discretization parameter (![][image56]). | Bypasses the structural rigidity and aliasing of spatial embeddings. |
| **Nanosecond Precision** | Prone to severe floating-point precision loss and aliasing without aggressive scaling. | Natively managed via continuous, mathematically stable decay functions. | Preserves sub-microsecond event ordering required for detecting ultra-fast cyber anomalies. |

## **Conclusion**

The Temporal Graph Network (TGN) framework remains a foundational pillar in the mathematical modeling of continuous-time dynamic graphs. By introducing per-node compressed memory states, paired with an elegant Raw Message Store to navigate the complex paradox of chronological batching and information leakage, TGN definitively proved that Graph Neural Networks could effectively model dynamic systems in real-time. The architecture's ability to update node representations asynchronously upon the arrival of new interactions established a rigorous standard for temporal graph learning.  
However, an exhaustive analysis of TGN reveals profound structural boundaries that limit its application in extreme computational environments. Its reliance on pairwise message aggregation strips away the rich, multi-entity context required to track systemic behavior accurately. Furthermore, the inherent mathematical limitations of recurrent memory updaters (GRUs) create insurmountable hurdles when attempting to retain long-term dependencies over extended sequences of dense activity. Finally, its functional approach to time encoding, while theoretically robust under normal conditions, faces severe mechanical failure when forced to resolve the extreme variance of nanosecond-level granularities.  
For highly complex, high-velocity datasets such as system provenance logs, moving beyond TGN is not merely an optimization—it is a computational and theoretical necessity. By substituting pairwise edges with dynamic hyperedges, the architecture can preserve atomic multi-entity interactions and propagate state naturally through shared infrastructure objects. By replacing the GRU memory module with Mamba's continuous State-Space formulation, the system can leverage hardware-aware selective scans to process infinite event sequences in parallel, linear time. Most critically, utilizing the exact time interval as a continuous control parameter for state discretization entirely bypasses the brittleness of static trigonometric time embeddings, enabling fluid, mathematically sound processing of nanosecond dynamics. This evolutionary architectural step bridges the gap between traditional dynamic graph learning and the stringent demands of hyperscale, continuous-time anomaly detection.
